# Gravitational Potential Energy

## Gravitational potential energy

> **Spec point** — `1.7.3` · Recall and use the equation for the change in gravitational potential energy ∆Ep = mg∆h

## Gravitational potential energy

### Extended Tier Only

- Energy in an object's gravitational potential energy store is defined as:

**The energy an object has due to its height in a gravitational field**

- [Work is done against the weight force](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/physics/cie/23/revision-notes/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-7-energy-work-and-power/1-7-5-work-done/?_ai=internal-linking) exerted on the object; therefore, energy is transferred
- This means that:

  - if an object is **lifted **up, energy will be transferred **to** its gravitational potential energy store
  - if an object is **lowered**, energy will be transferred **away from** its gravitational potential energy store

![A mass being lifted vertically through a gravitational field, with the increase in height marked, showing energy transferred to its gravitational potential energy store.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/a873674681ac-1-7-3-gravitational-potential-energy-cie-igcse-2.png)

*Energy is transferred to the mass's gravitational potential energy store as it is lifted through the gravitational field*

### Gravitational potential energy equation

- The change in energy in an object's gravitational potential energy store can be calculated using the equation:

$\DeltaE_{p}=mg\Deltah$

- Where:

  - $\DeltaE_{p}$ = change in gravitational potential energy, measured in joules (J)
  - $m$ = mass, measured in kilograms (kg)
  - $g$ = gravitational field strength, measured in newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
  - $\Deltah$ = change in height, measured in metres (m)
- When two heights are given, the difference between the heights must be used since $\Deltah$ is the change in height

- When an object is moved vertically a gravitational field, the work done on the object is **equal** to the increase in its gravitational potential energy store

> **Exam Hint**
> Note that $\Deltah$ is always the change in **vertical** height, not the distance travelled along a slope or ramp.
> 
> Remember that the change in gravitational potential energy has units of joules (J). Any mass given in grams must be converted into kilograms before substituting.

> **Worked Example**
> A man climbs a flight of stairs that is, in total, 3.0 m higher than the floor. The man has a mass of 72 kg, and the gravitational field strength on Earth is approximately 9.8 N/kg.
> 
> Calculate the energy transferred to the man's gravitational potential energy store.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> **Step 1: List the known quantities**
> 
> - Mass of the man, $m=72\mathrm{kg}$
> - Gravitational field strength, $g=9.8N/\mathrm{kg}$
> - Change in height, $\Deltah=3.0m$
> 
> **Step 2: Write down the equation for gravitational potential energy**
> 
> $\DeltaE_{p}=mg\Deltah$
> 
> **Step 3: Calculate the gravitational potential energy**
> 
> $\DeltaE_{p}=72\times9.8\times3.0$
> 
> $\DeltaE_{p}=2116.8J$
> 
> **Step 4: Round to an appropriate number of significant figures**
> 
> - The input values are to 2 s.f. so the answer is also given to 2 s.f.
> 
> $\Delta E_{p}  =  2100  J  \left(2  s . f .\right)$

> **Exam Hint**
> In your IGCSE exam, you will generally be expected to round your answers to an appropriate number of significant figures. In theory papers, any answer given to two or more significant figures is accepted unless the question says otherwise.
> 
> Your answer can only be as precise as your least precise input value. Therefore, your final answer should round to the lowest number of significant figures of all your input values.

title: Conservation of Energy
bodyMd:
# Conservation of Energy

## Conservation of energy

> **Spec point** — `1.7.4` · Know the principle of the conservation of energy and apply this principle to simple examples including the interpretation of simple flow diagrams

## Conservation of energy

- The **principle of conservation of energy** states that:

**Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one store to another**

- The principle of conservation of energy means that for a closed system, the total amount of energy is **constant**
- The **total **amount of energy transferred **into **the system must be **equal **to the **total **amount of energy transferred **away **from the system

- Therefore, energy cannot be ‘lost’, but it can be transferred to the surroundings

  - Energy can be **dissipated** (spread out) to the surroundings by heating and radiation
  - Dissipated energy transfers are often not **useful**, in which case they can be described as [wasted energy](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/physics/cie/23/revision-notes/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-7-energy-work-and-power/1-7-7-efficiency/?_ai=internal-linking)

### Examples of the principle of conservation of energy

#### Example 1: a bat hitting a ball

- The moving bat has energy in its **kinetic **store
- Some of that energy is transferred **usefully** to the **kinetic** store of the ball
- Some of that energy is transferred from the **kinetic **store of the bat to the **thermal **store of the ball **mechanically **due to the impact of the bat on the ball

  - This energy transfer is not useful; the energy is **wasted**
- Some of that energy is **dissipated** by **heating** to the **thermal **store of the bat, the ball, and the surroundings

  - This energy transfer is not useful; the energy is **wasted**
- The total amount of energy transferred into the system is equal to the total amount of energy transferred away from the system

#### Conservation of energy: a bat hitting a ball

![An energy flow diagram showing energy transferred from the kinetic store of the bat to the kinetic store of the ball, with wasted energy transferred to the thermal stores of the bat, ball and surroundings.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/b1cf23a93531-bat-and-ball-energy-flow-diagram-new.png)

*Energy flow diagram showing energy transfers when a bat hits a ball*

![A bat striking a ball, with arrows showing the useful transfer to the ball's kinetic store and the wasted transfer by heating.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/3fce7a33ab6b-bat-and-ball-energy-transfer.png)

*The principle of conservation of energy applied to a bat hitting a ball*

#### Example 2: boiling water in a kettle

- When an electric kettle boils water, **energy** is transferred **electrically** from the mains supply to the **thermal store** of the heating element inside the kettle
- As the heating element gets hotter, **energy** is transferred **by heating** to the **thermal store** of the water

- Some of the energy is transferred to the **thermal** store of the plastic kettle

  - This energy transfer is not useful; the energy is **wasted**
- And some energy is **dissipated **to the **thermal store** of the surroundings due to the air around the kettle being heated

  - This energy transfer is not useful; the energy is wasted
- The total amount of energy transferred into the system is equal to the total amount of energy transferred away from the system

#### Conservation of energy: a kettle boiling water

![An electric kettle boiling water, showing energy transferred electrically from the thermal store of the kettle to the thermal store of the water.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/f29f45f90037-boiling-kettle-store-igcse-and-gcse-physics-revi.png)

*The principle of conservation of energy applied to a kettle boiling water*

> **Exam Hint**
> When describing wasted energy, always say which store it ends up in.*** ***

### Energy flow diagrams

- Energy stores and transfers can be represented using a flow diagram

  - This shows both the stores and the transfers taking place within a system

![Diagram of a nuclear power station showing reactor, steam generator, turbine and generator, with energy transfers from uranium fuel to the National Grid.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/c3fd1995da50-1-7-4-conservation-of-energy-flow-diagram.png)

*Energy flow diagram for a nuclear power plant. Stores are shown in labelled boxes and transfer pathways as arrows between them*

- In an energy flow diagram, energy is always **conserved**

**total energy in = total energy out**

> **Exam Hint**
> This is a useful way to do calculations, but it is **not** a statement of the principle of conservation of energy — if a question asks you to state the principle, you must say that energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one store to another.
> 
> Note that you may be asked to fill in missing labels in energy flow diagrams.

> **Worked Example**
> The diagram shows a rollercoaster going down a track.
> 
> The rollercoaster takes the path A → B → C → D.
> 
> ![Diagram of a rollercoaster truck on a curved track labelled A, passing around a circular loop labelled B at the start of the loop and C at the end of the loop, then continuing onto a horizontal track D.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/f4f9667c6b9d-we-energy-transfers-question-image.png)
> 
> Which statement is true about the energy changes that occur for the rollercoaster down this track?
> 
> **A.**     *E*<sub>K</sub> → Δ*E*<sub>P</sub> → Δ*E*<sub>P</sub> → *E*<sub>K</sub>
> 
> **B.**     *E*<sub>K</sub> → Δ*E*<sub>P</sub> → *E*<sub>K</sub> → Δ*E*<sub>P</sub>
> 
> **C.**     Δ*E*<sub>P</sub> → *E*<sub>K</sub> → *E*<sub>K</sub> → Δ*E*<sub>P</sub>
> 
> **D.**     Δ*E*<sub>P</sub> → *E*<sub>K</sub> → Δ*E*<sub>P</sub> → *E*<sub>K</sub>
> 
> [1]
> 
> **Answer: **
> 
> - **At point A:**
> 
>   - The rollercoaster is raised above the ground, therefore it has energy in its **gravitational potential store**
> 
> - **At point B:**
> 
>   - As it travels down the track towards B, energy is transferred **mechanically** to its **kinetic store **
> 
> - **At point C:**
> 
>   - Energy is transferred **mechanically **from the** **kinetic store** **to the** gravitational potential store**
>   - As the kinetic energy store **empties**, the gravitational potential energy store **fills**
> 
> - **At point D:**
> 
>   - Energy is transferred **mechanically **from the gravitational potential store to the **kinetic store**
>   - The flat terrain means there is no change in the amount of energy in its gravitational potential store, the rollercoaster only has** **energy in its** kinetic store**
>   - The kinetic energy store is full
> - Therefore, the energy changes that occur for the rollercoaster down this track is given by **D**: Δ*E*<sub>P</sub> → *E*<sub>K</sub> → Δ*E*<sub>P</sub> → *E*<sub>K </sub>**[1 mark]**
> 
> - In reality, some energy will also be transferred to the thermal energy store of the tracks due to **friction**, and away from the system by **sound**
> - This energy is described as **dissipated to the surroundings**
> 
>   - The total amount of energy in the system will be constant
>   - Total energy in = total energy out

> **Exam Hint**
> It is helpful to think of energy stores as beakers and the total energy in the system as water. The water can be poured from one beaker into another, back and forth, as energy is transferred between stores.
> 
> You may not always be given the energy transfers happening in the system in your IGCSE exam questions.
> 
> By familiarising yourself with the energy stores and transfer pathways, you should be able to relate these to the situation presented in the question. For example, a ball rolling down a hill transfers energy from the ball's gravitational potential energy store to its kinetic energy store mechanically, while a spring transfers energy from its elastic potential energy store to its kinetic energy store mechanically.

## Sankey diagrams

> **Spec point** — `1.7.4` · Know the principle of the conservation of energy and apply this principle to complex examples involving multiple stages, including the interpretation of Sankey diagrams

## Sankey diagrams

### Extended Tier Only

- **Sankey diagrams** can be used to represent energy transfers

- Sankey diagrams are characterised by arrows that split to show the proportions of the energy transfers taking place

- The different parts of the arrow in a Sankey diagram represent the different energy transfers:

  - The left-hand side of the arrow (the flat end) represents the energy transferred **into **the system
  - The straight arrow pointing to the right represents the energy that ends up in the desired store; this is the **useful energy output**
  - The arrows that bend away represent the **wasted energy**

![A labelled Sankey diagram showing the total energy input on the left, the useful energy output continuing ahead, and the wasted energy branching away.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/97d1ceb3c755-8-1-2-sankey-diagram-demonstration-sl-physics-rn.png)

*Total energy in, wasted energy and useful energy out shown on a Sankey diagram *

- The width of each arrow is **proportional **to the amount of energy being transferred
- As a result of the conservation of energy:

**total energy in = total energy out**

**total energy in = useful energy out + wasted energy**

- A Sankey diagram for a modern efficient light bulb will look very different from that for an old filament light bulb
- A more efficient light bulb has **less** wasted energy

  - This is shown by the smaller arrow downwards representing the energy transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings

![Two Sankey diagrams side by side, showing an energy-efficient bulb with a narrow wasted-energy branch and a filament bulb with a much wider wasted-energy branch.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/4ed1d0700af2-cie-igcse-1-7-4-phy-rn-sankey-comparison-new.png)

*Sankey diagrams showing filament bulbs have a much greater proportion of wasted energy than modern energy efficient bulbs*

> **Worked Example**
> An electric motor is used to lift a weight. The diagram represents the energy transfers in the system.
> 
> ![A Sankey diagram with 500 J of input energy, 120 J of energy transferred to the weight and wasted energy.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/462fe2156d21-3-1-3-we-sankey-question-image.png)
> 
> Calculate the amount of wasted energy.
> 
> [2]
> 
> **Answer: **
> 
> **Step 1: State the conservation of energy**
> 
> - Energy cannot be created or destroyed, it can only be transferred from one store to another
> 
> $\mathrm{total} \mathrm{energy} \mathrm{in}=\mathrm{useful} \mathrm{energy} \mathrm{out}+\mathrm{wasted} \mathrm{energy}$
> 
> **Step 2: Rearrange the equation for the wasted energy**
> 
> $\mathrm{wasted} \mathrm{energy}=\mathrm{total} \mathrm{energy} \mathrm{in}-\mathrm{useful} \mathrm{energy} \mathrm{out}$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Step 3: Substitute the values from the diagram**
> 
> $\mathrm{wasted} \mathrm{energy}=500-120$
> 
> $\mathrm{wasted} \mathrm{energy}=380J$ **[1 mark]**

> **Exam Hint**
> Since arrow width is proportional to the amount of energy being transferred, scaled diagrams and grid lines can be used to measure the amount of energy represented by an arrow.
> 
> When energy is wasted in more than one way on a Sankey diagram, remember to add each wasted arrow to get the total wasted energy.

title: Work Done
bodyMd:
# Work Done

## Work done & energy transfers

> **Spec point** — `1.7.5` · Understand that mechanical or electrical work done is equal to the energy transferred
Recall and use the equation for mechanical working W = Fd = ∆E

## Work done & energy transfers

- **Mechanical work** is done when an object is moved over a **distance** by a **force** applied in the **direction** of its displacement

  - It is said that the **force does work** on the object
  - If a force is applied to an object but does not result in any movement, no work is done
- When **work **is done, **energy **is transferred
- Work done and energy transferred are **equivalent **quantities

![A person pushing a box along the ground, with an arrow showing the applied force and a second arrow showing the distance the box moves in the same direction.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/257ed8820c14-work-force-object.png)

*Work is done when a force is used to move an object over a distance, and energy is transferred from the person to the box*

### Work done equation

- The formula for work done is:

$W=Fd=\DeltaE$

- Where:

  - $W$ = work done, measured in joules (J)
  - $F$ = force applied, measured in newtons (N)
  - $d$ = distance moved in the direction of the force, measured in metres (m)
  - $\DeltaE$ = energy transferred, measured in joules (J)

- Mechanical work done and electrical work done are equivalent to energy transferred

$\mathrm{work} \mathrm{done}=\mathrm{energy} \mathrm{transferred}$

- Work done can also have units of newton-metres since:

$1Nm=1J$

### Examples of work done

- Work is done on a ball when it is lifted to a height:

  - A force is required to lift the ball
  - Work is done against the weight force to lift the ball through the gravitational field
  - Energy is transferred as work done

#### Work done lifting a ball

![A ball is lifted to a height above the ground. The weight of the ball is labelled and acts downwards.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/380d730eadbb-5-2-1-work-done-ball.png)

*Work is done against the ball's weight as it is lifted, transferring energy to its gravitational potential store *

- Work is done when a bird flies through the air

  - A force is required to overcome the drag force
  - Work is done against the drag force as the bird flies over a distance
  - Energy is transferred as work is done

#### Work done by a bird

![Diagram of a bird flying right above grass, with an arrow labelled “air resistance” pointing left and a horizontal arrow below showing distance travelled.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/c3bea2ecf35b-5-2-1-work-done-bird.png)

*The bird does work against air resistance (drag) as it flies through the air*

> **Worked Example**
> A car moving at speed begins to apply the brakes. The brakes of the car apply a force of 500 N, which brings it to a stop after 23 m.
> 
> ![A car braking to a stop, with an arrow showing the 500 N braking force acting opposite to its motion over 23 m.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/34727e658289-braking-work.png)
> 
> Calculate the work done by the brakes in stopping the car.
> 
> [2]
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> **Step 1: List the known quantities**
> 
> - Distance, $d=23m$
> - Force, $F=500N$
> 
> **Step 2: Write out the work done equation**
> 
> $W=Fd$
> 
> **Step 3: Calculate the work done on the car by the brakes**
> 
> $W=500\times23$* ***[1 mark]**
> 
> $W=11500J$* ***[1 mark]**

> **Exam Hint**
> Remember to always convert the distance into **metres** and force into **newtons** so that the work done, which is equal to force **multiplied** by the distance moved in the direction of the force, is in **joules**.
> 
> In addition, remember that work done is **equivalent** to energy transferred. For example, the work done by a force will usually describe a change in kinetic energy or gravitational potential energy of an object.

## Energy, Work & Power Video

> **Spec point** — `1.7.5` · nan

title: Power
bodyMd:
# Power

## Power

> **Spec point** — `1.7.6` · Define power as work done per unit time and also as energy transferred per unit time; recall the equations
   (a) P = W/t
   (b) P = ∆E/t

## Power

- Power is defined as:

**Work done** **per unit time**

- Since [work done is equal to energy transferred](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/physics/cie/23/revision-notes/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-7-energy-work-and-power/1-7-5-work-done/?_ai=internal-linking), **power **is also defined as:

**Energy transferred** **per unit time**

- Machines, such as car engines, transfer energy from one energy store to another constantly over a period of **time**

  - The **rate **of this energy transfer, or the rate of work done, is **power**
- **Time **is an important consideration when it comes to **power**

### Two cars with different power ratings doing the same amount of work

- Two cars transfer the **same amount of energy **or do the **same amount of work **to accelerate over a distance
- If one car has **more power**, it will transfer that energy, or do that work, in a **shorter amount of time**

![Two cars accelerating to the same final speed, with the more powerful car reaching that speed in less time.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/ba280ab6f9bd-power-cars.png)

*Two cars accelerate to the same final speed, but the one with more power will reach that speed sooner*

### Two motors with different power ratings doing the same amount of work

- Two electric motors:

  - lift the same weight
  - by the same height
  - but one motor lifts it **faster** than the other
- The motor that lifts the weight faster has more **power**

![Two electric motors lifting identical weights through the same height, with the more powerful motor completing the lift in less time.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/de02148a6e20-1-1-10-electric-motors-power.png)

*Two motors with different powers*

### Power ratings

- **Power ratings** are given to appliances to show the amount of energy transferred per unit time
- Common power ratings are shown in the table below:

#### Power ratings table

| **Appliance** | **Power rating** |
|---|---|
| A torch | 1 W |
| An electric light bulb | 100 W |
| An electric oven | 10 000 W = 10 kW |
| A train | 1 000 000 W = 1 MW |
| Large power station | 1$\times$10<sup>9</sup> W |
| Global power demand | 1$\times$10<sup>13</sup> W |
| A star like the Sun | 1$\times$10<sup>26</sup> W |

- 1 kW = 1000 W = 1$\times$10<sup>3</sup> W (1 kilowatt = 1000 watts)
- 1 MW = 1 000 000 W = 1$\times$10<sup>6</sup> W (1 megawatt = 1 million watts)

## Calculating power

> **Spec point** — `1.7.6` · use the equations
   (a) P = W/t
   (b) P = ∆E/t

## Calculating power

### The power equations

- There are two equivalent forms of the power equation
- Power can be expressed in terms of work done $W$:

$P=\frac{W}{t}$

- Or, power can be expressed in terms of energy transferred $\DeltaE$:

$P=\frac{\DeltaE}{t}$

- Where:

  - $P$* *= power measured in watts (W)
  - $W$* = *work done, measured in joules (J)
  - $t$ = time measured in seconds (s)
  - $\DeltaE$ = energy transferred, measured in joules (J)

- Note that these two equations may be written slightly differently, but they represent the same thing

  - A transfer of energy (work done) over time
- From this equation, 1 W is equivalent to 1 J/s

> **Worked Example**
> Calculate the energy transferred when an iron with a power rating of 2000 W is used for 5 minutes.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> **Step 1: List the known values**
> 
> - Power, $P=2000W$
> - Time, $t=5\mathrm{minutes}$
> 
> **Step 2: Convert minutes into seconds**
> 
> - $1\mathrm{min}=60s$
> 
> $5\mathrm{min}=5\times60=300s$
> 
> **Step 3: Write down the power equation in terms of energy**
> 
> $P=\frac{\DeltaE}{t}$
> 
> **Step 4: Rearrange to make energy transferred, Δ*****E, the subject***
> 
> $\DeltaE=Pt$
> 
> **Step 5: Substitute in the known values**
> 
> $\DeltaE=2000\times300$
> 
> $\DeltaE=600000J$

> **Exam Hint**
> Remember to convert time into **seconds** when calculating a power in watts.
> 
> Think of power as “energy per second”. Thinking of it this way will help you to remember the relationship between power and energy and which two quantities are needed to calculate power.
> 
> In your IGCSE exam, you will be expected to use both equations and to be able to rearrange them. You may be required to calculate the energy transferred in a previous question part, so always check back through the question if you seem to be missing a value.

title: Efficiency
bodyMd:
# Efficiency

## Efficiency of energy transfer

> **Spec point** — `1.7.7` · Understand, qualitatively, the concept of efficiency of energy transfer

## Efficiency of energy transfer

- The **efficiency **of a system is a measure of the amount of **useful **and **wasted energy** in an energy transfer
- Efficiency is defined as:

**The ratio of the useful power or energy output from a system to its total power or energy input**

- If a system has **high** efficiency, this means most of the energy transferred is **useful**
- If a system has **low** efficiency, this means most of the energy transferred is **wasted**

  - If a lamp is 25% efficient, this means that 25% of the energy supplied to it is transferred usefully as light, and the other 75% is wasted.
- **No** system reaches 100% efficiency

  - Energy is **always** wasted into other non-useful forms, such as sound and thermal energy which is lost to the surroundings (often due to friction)

## Calculating efficiency

> **Spec point** — `1.7.7` · Define efficiency as: 
   (a) (%) efficiency = (useful energy output)/(total energy input) (× 100%) 
   (b) (%) efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input) (× 100%)
recall and use these equations

## Calculating efficiency

### Extended Tier Only

- Efficiency can be calculated using two equations

- Efficiency in terms of **energy**:

$efficiency  =  \frac{useful  energy  output}{total  energy  input}  \left(\times 100 \%\right)$

- Efficiency in terms of **power**:

$efficiency  =  \frac{useful  power  output}{total  power  input}  \left(\times 100 \%\right)$

- Efficiency can be given as a decimal between 0 and 1, or as a percentage between 0 and 100%.

- In the production of electricity:

  - Energy is used to heat water to produce steam
  - The steam turns a turbine
  - The turbine turns a generator
  - The generator produces electricity
  
    - At each stage of this process, energy is dissipated to the surroundings
- The overall efficiency of a typical thermal power station is approximately 30%

  - This means that about 70% of the energy from the fuel is **wasted** inside the power station, mostly as thermal energy transferred to the surroundings, and only about 30% is transferred **usefully** as electrical energy

![A Sankey diagram for a gas-fired power station, showing the chemical energy input branching into a narrow useful electrical output and three wider wasted thermal energy arrows.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/01a5113d7af6-cie-1-8-6-sankey-diagram-of-power-station-effici.png)

*Sankey diagram showing the energy transfers involved in generating electricity in a gas-fired power station*

> **Worked Example**
> An electric motor lifts a 7.2 kg load through a height of 5.0 m in 3 seconds. The efficiency of the motor is 35%.
> 
> Calculate the power supplied to the motor.
> 
> [4]
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> **Step 1: List the known quantities**
> 
> - Mass of load, $m$ = 7.2 kg
> - Change in height, $h$ = 5.0 m
> - Gravitational field strength, $g$ = 9.8 N/kg
> - Time, $t$ = 3 s
> - Efficiency = 35% or 0.35
> 
> **Step 2: Calculate the power output of the motor**
> 
> - The useful energy output is the work done in lifting the load
> - The useful power output is that energy divided by the time taken
> 
> $\mathrm{power} \mathrm{output}=\frac{\DeltaE}{t}$
> 
> - $\DeltaE$ is equal to the change in gravitational potential energy as the load is lifted
> 
> $\DeltaE_{P}=mg\Deltah$
> 
> $\DeltaE_{P}=7.2\times9.8\times5.0=352.8J$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Therefore:
> 
> $\mathrm{power} \mathrm{output}=\frac{352.8}{3}=117.6W$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Step 3: Write down the efficiency equation in terms of power**
> 
> $\mathrm{efficiency}=\frac{\mathrm{useful} \mathrm{power} \mathrm{output}}{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{power} \mathrm{input}}$
> 
> **Step 4: Rearrange to make power input the subject**
> 
> $\mathrm{power} \mathrm{input}=\frac{\mathrm{power} \mathrm{output}}{\mathrm{efficiency}}$
> 
> **Step 5: Substitute the values into the power input equation**
> 
> $\mathrm{power} \mathrm{input}=\frac{117.6}{0.35}$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> $\mathrm{power} \mathrm{input}=336W$ **[1 mark]**

> **Exam Hint**
> Efficiency can be given in a decimal (between 0 and 1) or percentage format (between 0 and 100%)
> 
> If the answer is required as a percentage, remember to multiply the ratio by 100 to convert it:
> 
> - if the decimal = 0.25, percentage = 0.25 × 100 = 25%
> 
> Remember that efficiency is calculated using the **useful** energy or power output. Efficiency has **no units**, and can **never** exceed 100%.

## Efficiency video

> **Spec point** — `1.7.7` · nan

title: Energy from the Sun
bodyMd:
# Energy from the Sun

## The Sun

> **Spec point** — `1.8.1` · •  Know that radiation from the Sun is the main source of energy for all our energy resources except geothermal, nuclear and tidal

## The Sun

### Extended Tier Only

- The Sun transfers energy to Earth by **electromagnetic radiation**
- Most of our energy resources on Earth come indirectly from the **Sun**

  - The Sun heats up the atmosphere, creating **wind** and producing **waves**
  - Water evaporated by the Sun falls as rain, filling up **reservoirs**
  - Plants grown using sunlight form the basis for fuels – both biofuels and fossil fuels

- Some energy resources, however, do not come from the Sun
- These include:

  - **Geothermal **– this comes from thermal energy produced in the Earth’s core
  - **Nuclear **– this comes from elements which make up a small proportion of the Earth’s crust
  - **Tidal **– this comes (mainly) from the gravitational attraction of the Moon

![The Sun, the source of energy for most of Earth's energy resources.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/c1f002a75621-8-1-2-the-sun.png)

*Energy from the Sun is the source of the energy stored in many of Earth's energy resources*

## Solar cells

> **Spec point** — `1.8.1` · Describe how useful energy may be obtained, or electrical power generated, from: 
   *  light from the Sun to generate electrical power (solar cells)
Describe advantages and disadvantages in terms of renewability, availability, reliability, scale and environmental impact:

## Solar cells

- The energy from the Sun that falls on the Earth is transferred by radiation

  - Mostly **visible light** and **infrared radiation**
- The amount of energy transferred from the Sun to the Earth **each hour** is equal to the energy use of the world for **one year!**
- Therefore, scientists are working hard to find methods of harnessing this energy

  - Solar energy has a **low energy density**, which means large collecting devices are required
  - Collecting solar energy has been **expensive** (due to the equipment required) and **inefficient**
  - **Improved technology** and large-scale manufacturing have made solar cells much cheaper and more efficient than they used to be

- **Solar cells** transfer energy from sunlight and produce a current, therefore generating **electricity **

  - Solar cells, sometimes called photovoltaic cells, are made of semiconducting materials
  - A number of cells connected together can supply electricity to homes, small-scale businesses, communication devices and satellites
  - Energy generated from solar cells can be stored in batteries for later use

![An array of photovoltaic solar cells converting sunlight directly into electricity.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/b2159e1283fd-1-8-1-solar-cells-cie-igcse-23-rn.png)

*Solar cells use energy from sunlight to produce electricity*

### Advantages of solar cells

- Solar energy is a **renewable** resource since it relies on light from the Sun which will not run out

**A renewable resource is one which can be replenished at the same rate as it is used**

- Solar farms do not emit **carbon dioxide** or other greenhouse gases while operating, so they do not contribute to global warming
- Solar energy can be generated in **remote places** that are not connected to an electricity grid

  - For example, to power solar street signs in rural areas

- Solar farms have low running costs because there is no fuel to buy

### Disadvantages of solar cells

- Solar cells provide an **intermittent or unreliable** supply of electricity because they depend entirely on the availability of sunlight

  - They cannot generate electrical power at night, and their power output is heavily **dependent** on weather conditions
- Solar farms need to be large-scale and contain vast numbers of solar cells to produce large amounts of electricity
- Each solar cell generally has a **lower** power output than a standard mains electrical supply

## Solar panels

> **Spec point** — `1.8.1` · Describe how useful energy may be obtained, or electrical power generated, from:  
 * infrared and other electromagnetic waves from the Sun to heat water (solar panels) and be the source of wind energy 
 including references to a boiler, turbine and generator where they are used
Describe advantages and disadvantages in terms of renewability, availability, reliability, scale and environmental impact

## Solar panels

- Useful energy may be obtained from infrared and other electromagnetic waves from the Sun using **solar panels**

- **Solar panels** transfer energy from sunlight to the thermal store of the solar panels, which is used to **heat water** in the pipes

  - Solar panels can be used to warm domestic water supplies
  - This can reduce the cost of producing hot water since it is heated partially by the solar panels
- **Solar furnaces** consist of large curved mirrors that focus the Sun's rays onto a small area

  - These can be used to boil water, generating enough steam to turn turbines and generate electricity in a power station

![A solar panel with water pipes running through it connected to a storage tank.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/8c0d2c9ceba3-1-8-1-solar-panel-cie-igcse-23-rn.png)

*Solar panels use energy from sunlight to heat water *

### How solar panels work

- Water is **stored **in a water **tank **and pumped through small **pipes **running through the solar panel
- I**nfrared radiation** from the Sun heats the water in the pipes as it flows through them
- The water returns to the tank at a** higher temperature**
- Water may still need to be heated further to reach the desired temperature (e.g. for a shower)

### Advantages of solar panels

- Solar energy is a **renewable** resource since it relies on light from the Sun which will not run out
- Solar panels do not emit **carbon dioxide** or other greenhouse gases while operating, so they do not contribute to global warming
- While they may have an initial installation cost, they are **cheap to run** and require **low maintenance**
- Solar panels can be placed on the roofs of buildings, saving ground space

### Disadvantages of solar panels

- Solar panels provide an **intermittent or unreliable** supply of electricity because they depend entirely on the availability of sunlight
- Solar furnaces need to be large-scale to produce high temperatures
- Solar panels have a much lower power output compared to a standard mains electrical supply

  - A solar panel will take **longer to recharge a battery** than a mains supply would

## Wind energy

> **Spec point** — `1.8.1` · Describe how useful energy may be obtained, or electrical power generated, from:  
 * infrared and other electromagnetic waves from the Sun to heat water (solar panels) and be the source of wind energy 
 including references to a boiler, turbine and generator where they are used
Describe advantages and disadvantages in terms of renewability, availability, reliability, scale and environmental impact

## Wind energy

- Energy from the **wind **can be used to generate **electricity**
- The wind turns a **turbine**, which turns a **generator**, which generates electricity
- Energy from the kinetic store of the wind is transferred

  - mechanically to the kinetic store of the turbine
  - which is transferred mechanically to the kinetic store of the generator
  - which is transferred electrically to the electricity grid

![A wind farm with several turbines.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/8e633cc1fa2a-wind-farm.bin)

*Wind turbines use energy from the wind to generate electricity*

### Advantages of wind power

- Wind is a **renewable **resource
- Wind turbines do not emit **carbon dioxide** or other greenhouse gases while operating, so they do not contribute to global warming
- Wind turbines do not produce **sulfur dioxide** or other acidic gases during operation, so they do not contribute to acid rain
- **Offshore** wind farms can be built in coastal areas
- Wind turbines do not use fuel, so there are no fuel costs

### Disadvantages of wind power

- Wind power is **not reliable** because the wind does not blow constantly, and they cannot generate power if the wind is too weak or too strong
- Each turbine only produces a **small** amount of electricity, so wind farms are needed for large-scale electricity generation
- Wind turbines are often **difficult to maintain**, particularly if they are built offshore
- Offshore wind farms can **disrupt shipping** routes

> **Exam Hint**
> In your IGCSE exam, you will **not** be awarded marks for giving vague advantages or disadvantages without further explanation. Make sure you can justify your answers.

title: Energy from Fuels
bodyMd:
# Energy from Fuels

## Fossil fuels

> **Spec point** — `1.8.2` · Describe how useful energy may be obtained, or electrical power generated, from:  
 * chemical energy stored in fossil fuels 
 including references to a boiler, turbine and generator where they are used
Describe advantages and disadvantages in terms of renewability, availability, reliability, scale and environmental impact

## Fossil fuels

- Fossil fuels are:

  - **Coal**
  - **Natural gas** (mostly methane)
  - Crude **oil** which is refined into petrol, diesel and other fuels

![Coal, oil and natural gas, the three fossil fuels.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/eae79e2c0367-1-8-2-fossil-fuels-cie-igcse-23-rn.png)

*Fossil fuels: coal, oil and natural gas*

- Fossil fuels are formed from the **remains of plants and animals **
- **Chemical energy** stored in fossil fuels originally came from **sunlight**

  - Energy from the Sun was transferred to the chemical energy store of plants by photosynthesis (plants use energy from sunlight to make food)
  - Animals ate the plants and the energy was transferred to their chemical store

### Advantages of fossil fuels

- Fossil fuel power stations are **extremely reliable** since they can burn fossil fuels on demand and the infrastructure is well established in most countries

  - Energy output is **not dependent** on weather conditions
- Fossil fuel power stations are **extremely responsive** (they can be turned on and off easily), which means they can meet the changing demands of a nation
- Fossil fuels are relatively **safe **to store and use

### Disadvantages of fossil fuels

- It takes **millions of years** for fossil fuels to form

  - This is why they are considered to be a **non-renewable** energy resource
  - The increasing demand for a **decreasing supply** causes prices to increase
  - Fossil fuels are being used far faster than they form, so supplies are **finite** and will become increasingly difficult and expensive to extract.
- Burning fossil fuels pollutes the atmosphere with harmful gases such as:

  - **Carbon dioxide** which contributes to the **greenhouse effect**
  - **Sulfur dioxide** which produces **acid rain**
  - Both carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide can be captured upon burning, preventing them from being released into the atmosphere but this is expensive to do
- Extraction of fossil fuels causes **damage **to the **environment**

### Uses of fossil fuels

- Fossil fuels are used for:

  - Transport
  - Generating electricity
  - Heating

#### Transport

- The majority of vehicles in the world are powered by **petroleum** products such as petrol, diesel and kerosene

  - These resources all originate from crude oil, which is a **fossil fuel**
- A growing number of vehicles are now being powered by **electricity**

- The advantage of this is that while the vehicle is being driven, it produces **zero carbon emissions**
- The disadvantage is that when the vehicle is being charged, it is connected to the electricity grid, which currently uses a **combination** of renewable and non-renewable energy sources

#### Electricity generation

- Fossil fuels, such as **gas **and **coal**, are used to produce energy **on-demand** when energy is needed

  - The fossil fuel is burned (combusted) and used to heat water to produce **steam**
  - The steam turns a **turbine**
  - The turbine turns a **generator**, which generates electricity
  - The current produced is transmitted via the **electricity grid**
  - The steam is condensed into water to be used again

#### Electricity generation in a coal-fired power station

![A coal-fired power station, showing coal burned in a boiler to make steam, the steam turning a turbine, and the turbine turning a generator.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/cf16037ebb34-8-1-5-fossil-fuel-power-plant-sl-physics-rn.png)

*Fossil fuels are burned to heat water to produce steam. The steam turns the turbine, which turns the generator, which produces electricity*

- Electricity plays a bigger role in people's lives than ever before

  - With almost 8 billion people in the world, this means the **demand** for electricity is **extremely high**
  - To keep up with this demand, a combination of **all** the energy resources available is needed

#### Global energy consumption

![A chart of world energy consumption in 2019, showing oil 33%, natural gas 24%, coal 27%, nuclear energy 4% and renewables at 12%.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/8e1aec55edd1-1-2-1-world-energy-consumption-2019.png)

*In 2019, fossil fuels supplied around 80% of the world's primary energy. Burning them raises the level of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, which contributes to global warming*

#### Heating

- The majority of heating systems run on **fossil fuels**

  - **Gas **central heating systems are the most common, with a gas boiler that heats water through a system of pipes and radiators throughout the building
  - Boilers can also be powered by **oil **or biofuels
  - Open fireplaces burn wood or **coal**
- Electric heaters run on electricity
- Bottled gas can also be used in portable heaters

  - Bottled gas is either **propane **or **butane **which are also produced from fossil fuels

## Biofuels

> **Spec point** — `1.8.2` · Describe how useful energy may be obtained, or electrical power generated, from:  
 * chemical energy stored in biofuels
 including references to a boiler, turbine and generator where they are used
Describe advantages and disadvantages in terms of renewability, availability, reliability, scale and environmental impact

## Biofuels

- Biofuels are made from plant matter

  - Energy from sunlight is transferred to the **chemical store** of plants
- **Ethanol** or **methane** can be produced and used in place of fossil fuels

  - However, they have only half the **energy density** of fossil fuels

![The biofuel cycle, showing plants absorbing carbon dioxide as they grow, plant crops are then used for biofuel production which is used in cars.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/02a15a7f9d9f-1-8-2-biofuels-cie-igcse-23-rn.png)

*Plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis, but carbon dioxide is released back into the atmosphere when biofuels are burned*

### Advantages of biofuel

- Biofuel is a **renewable resource** since new plants can always be grown
- Biofuels provide a **reliable** and consistent supply of energy because the fuel can be stored and burned in a boiler whenever the electricity is needed
- Biofuel is generally considered to be **carbon neutral**

  - Although burning biofuels releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, the plants used to make the fuel take in carbon dioxide when they photosynthesise
- No **sulfur dioxide** is produced, so biofuels do not contribute to acid rain
- Some vehicles can be powered by **biofuel **rather than using fossil fuels
- Biofuel is added to petrol and diesel products in many countries to **reduce **the volume of **pollutants **released in combustion

### Disadvantages of biofuel

- Crops of biofuel-producing plants must be grown, which takes **time**

  - Growing the crops takes a lot of **land**, and takes **resources **needed for food production

- Burning biofuels releases **carbon dioxide** into the atmosphere

  - If the land had been used to grow crops for food, the same amount of carbon would have been taken out of the atmosphere, and much less carbon would have been returned
- Biofuels have only half the energy density of fossil fuels, which means twice as much fuel needs to be used to release the same amount of energy
- Not many vehicles can run on biofuel alone

## Nuclear fuel

> **Spec point** — `1.8.2` · Describe how useful energy may be obtained, or electrical power generated, from:  
 * nuclear fuel
 including references to a boiler, turbine and generator where they are used
Describe advantages and disadvantages in terms of renewability, availability, reliability, scale and environmental impact

## Nuclear fuel

- Energy stored in the **nucleus** of atoms can be released when the nucleus is broken in two

  - This is known as [nuclear fission](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/physics/cie/23/revision-notes/5-nuclear-physics/5-1-the-nuclear-model-of-the-atom/5-1-4-fission-and-fusion/?_ai=internal-linking)

![Diagram of uranium nuclear fission: an incoming neutron splits a uranium nucleus into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and two extra neutrons.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/69377017370b-1-8-2-fission-cie-igcse-23-rn.png)

*Nuclear Fission: when a large nucleus is broken into two smaller nuclei, energy is released*

- Nuclear power stations use fission reactions to **heat water** to produce steam, to turn turbines that turn generators which** generate electricity**

### Advantages of nuclear power

- Nuclear power stations do **not** emit carbon dioxide or sulfur dioxide during operation, so they do not contribute to global warming or acid rain
- Nuclear power stations are** extremely reliable** since nuclear fuel can be used on demand and stations are **well established** in some countries
- Nuclear power stations are **responsive **as the output is easily controlled
- Nuclear fuel has a **high energy density**

  - A small amount of fuel releases **massive amounts** of energy

### Disadvantages of nuclear power

- Nuclear power is a **non-renewable** resource

  - Uranium ore is mined from rocks so there is a **finite supply**
- Nuclear fuels produce **radioactive waste**

  - Radioactive waste is packaged and buried underground to be stored for **thousands **of years
  - Burial sites must remain undisturbed and uninhabited
- There are severe environmental consequences and risks of mutations or cancer if there is a radioactive leak, meaning **heavy containment** is necessary
- Nuclear power stations are **extremely expensive to build **and to decommission (close down)
- There is a high cost associated with maintaining **safe storage** facilities for the radioactive waste

> **Exam Hint**
> In your IGCSE exam, you may be required to discuss the advantages and disadvantages of various energy resources. Advantages and disadvantages must be specific and have an explanation. You may also need to apply your understanding of energy resources to unfamiliar scenarios, for example, by suggesting which type of energy resource would be best for a particular community. Make sure you can justify your choices.

title: Energy from Water
bodyMd:
# Energy from Water

## Wave and tide power

> **Spec point** — `1.8.3` · Describe how useful energy may be obtained, or electrical power generated, from:  
 * energy stored in waves and tides
 including references to a boiler, turbine and generator where they are used
Describe advantages and disadvantages in terms of renewability, availability, reliability, scale and environmental impact 

## Wave & tide power

- Energy can be obtained from the kinetic store of the waves and tides
- The motion of the water is used to turn a turbine, which turns a generator, which generates electricity

### Wave power

- Wave power uses devices that float on or near the surface
- The up-and-down motion of the waves drives a generator, either directly or by forcing air through a turbine

#### Turbines using wave power

![1-8-3-tidal-power-cie-igcse-23-rn](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/30822d4c2ca7-1-8-3-tidal-power-cie-igcse-23-rn.png)

*Underwater turbines generate electricity*

### Tidal power

- Tidal power uses tidal barrages to store water at a height as the tide comes in and goes out
- When the barrage is opened, water flows through a channel over a turbine

#### Tidal barrage

![A tidal barrage across an estuary, with water held at a height on one side and flowing through a turbine in the barrage wall.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/bf4a4a25005e-1-8-3-a-tidal-barrage-produces-elelctricity-usin.png)

*A tidal barrage stores water at a height and then opens a gate allowing water to flow over a turbine*

### Advantages of wave and tidal power

- Wave and tidal power are **renewable **energy resources
- Wave and tide power produce **no carbon dioxide** or greenhouse gases as no fuel is needed
- Tides are regular, so **tidal power** is **reliable **and predictable
- There are no fuel costs involved in wave and tidal power stations so running costs are **low**

### Disadvantages of wave and tidal power

- Wave power is **not available at all times **as the waves are not always large enough to turn the turbines
- Tidal barrages are built in **estuaries **so there are not many suitable locations around the world that are suitable for tidal power generation
- Because the equipment is submerged in the sea, underwater **maintenance** is more difficult
- The underwater turbines and tidal barrages can **interfere **with shipping routes and cause **damage **to habitats
- Wave and tidal power stations have a **long construction time** compared to some other power station types

> **Exam Hint**
> Tidal power is reliable **and** predictable because low and high tide cycles are easy to forecast. Wave power is less predictable due to changing wave speeds.

## Hydroelectric dams

> **Spec point** — `1.8.3` · Describe how useful energy may be obtained, or electrical power generated, from:  
 * water behind hydroelectric dams
 including references to a boiler, turbine and generator where they are used
Describe advantages and disadvantages in terms of renewability, availability, reliability, scale and environmental impact

## Hydroelectric dams

- When water is stored above ground level, it has energy in its **gravitational potential energy store**
- This energy can be transferred to the **kinetic energy store** if the water is allowed to flow down the slope
- Flowing water turns the turbine to **generate electricity**

![A hydroelectric dam with water stored behind it flowing down through a pipe and turning a turbine connected to a generator.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/04a0d55e5e62-1-8-3-hydroelectric-dam-cie-igcse-23-rn.png)

*A hydroelectric dam transfers energy mechanically from the gravitational potential energy store of the water to its kinetic energy store. The moving water turns the turbine*

### Advantages of hydroelectric power

- Hydroelectric power is **renewable** because the reservoir is refilled by rainfall
- Hyrdoelectric power does not contribute to **global warming** and does not produce **acid rain**
- Hydroelectric dams are **reliable **since water can be released on demand and dams are well established in most countries
- Hydroelectric power stations are **responsive **because they can be turned on and off easily to meet changing demand
- Hydroelectric power stations are **cheap to run** because there is no fuel to buy
- Hydroelectric power stations can produce **large **amounts of electricity

### Disadvantages of hydroelectric power

- Valleys are flooded to create the reservoir used to store the water, which **destroys habitats**, towns and villages
- There are **limited suitable sites** available for construction, as hydroelectric dams require both a steady water supply and the necessary vertical height
- Hydroelectric power stations are **expensive to build **because the land and properties need to be acquired in order to build the reservoir
- **Drought** can affect the supply of water
- **Pumping systems** are sometimes used to return the water to the reservoir

  - Pumped storage uses electricity from the grid to pump water back up to the reservoir, so its environmental impact depends on how that electricity was generated

title: Geothermal Energy
bodyMd:
# Geothermal Energy

## Geothermal energy

> **Spec point** — `1.8.4` · Describe how useful energy may be obtained, or electrical power generated, from:  
 * geothermal resources
 including references to a boiler, turbine and generator where they are used
Describe advantages and disadvantages in terms of renewability, availability, reliability, scale and environmental impact

## Geothermal energy

- **Tectonic activity** causes areas where the rocks below ground become **heated**
- Energy in the thermal store of the rocks can be obtained by:

  - Drilling **shafts **into the Earth's surface to expose the heated rocks
  - Injecting **water **into the shaft which is heated by the rocks
  - The water is returned via another shaft as **steam **or hot water
  - The steam turns a **turbine**, powering a **generator** that produces electricity.
  - The hot water can be used to heat homes and provide a **hot water** supply to households

![A geothermal power station, with cold water pumped down one shaft into hot rocks and returning as steam up a second shaft to turn a turbine and a generator.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/959549014813-1-8-4-geothermal-energy-cie-igcse-23-rn.png)

*Cold water is heated by the rocks and returned as hot water or steam, which can be used to generate electricity*

### Advantages of geothermal energy

- Geothermal energy is **renewable **— it comes from the long-term continuous decay of radioisotopes in the Earth's core that will outlive the Earth
- Geothermal power stations do not produce greenhouse gases (such as **carbon dioxide**) during operation and do not contribute to global warming
- Generating electricity from geothermal energy does not release acidic gases (such as **sulfur dioxide**) into the atmosphere and does not contribute to acid rain
- Geothermal power stations are **reliable **because the rocks remain hot for thousands of years so they can consistently produce electricity

### Disadvantages of geothermal energy

- Geothermal energy depends on tectonic activity, so there are **few suitable locations** on Earth
- Drilling can release gases trapped underground, including methane, which is a powerful **greenhouse gas**
- The initial cost to build the geothermal power station and drill deep into the Earth is extremely **expensive **
- Most geothermal power stations are **smaller** than fossil-fuel or nuclear stations

> **Exam Hint**
> Note that geothermal energy is one of three energy resources whose energy does **not** come from the Sun. The other two energy resources are nuclear energy (nuclear fission) and tidal energy.

title: Nuclear Fusion
bodyMd:
# Nuclear Fusion

## Nuclear fusion

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_CbN49GQxQnn7qzk6` · Know that energy is released by nuclear fusion in the Sun
Know that research is being carried out to investigate how energy released by nuclear fusion can be used to produce electrical energy on a large scale

## Nuclear fusion

### Extended Tier Only

- The Sun releases energy by the process of nuclear **fusion** in its core

  - Nuclear fusion is the process where two light atomic nuclei** join** together to create a heavier nucleus, releasing massive amounts of energy in the process
  - In the Sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse together to form helium nuclei

![Two nuclei join together to form a heavier nucleus, with energy released in the process.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/82526ac35b9a-nuclear-fusion.png)

*Fusion is the process in which small nuclei, such as hydrogen, are fused together to form larger nuclei, releasing energy in the process*

- It is **theoretically possible** to produce a **fusion reactor** that could be used to **generate electricity**

  - If this technology can be made to work at scale, it could supply very large amounts of electricity without producing carbon dioxide

- Fusion requires extremely **high temperatures **and **high pressures**, like in the centre of a star

  - This is to overcome the repulsive forces between nuclei
- Scientists are currently researching how to sustain a fusion reaction at lower temperatures

  - International research projects, funded mainly by governments working together, are making progress with some promising results
- Experiments have now released more energy from the fusion reaction than was delivered to the fuel, but not yet more than the total energy required to run the whole facility

  - Producing a sustained net energy gain remains the goal
  - If they succeed, virtually limitless amounts of energy could be produced, with large-scale, carbon-free electricity generation

> **Exam Hint**
> Note that fusion and fission are **different** processes. Nuclear fusion is the process where two light atomic nuclei join together to create a heavier nucleus. In contrast, nuclear fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei.

title: Pressure & Forces
bodyMd:
# Pressure & Forces

## Pressure

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_bcGp52BWd8qYh6nz` · Define pressure as force per unit area; recall and use the equation p = F/A
Describe how pressure varies with force and area in the context of everyday examples

## Pressure

### What is pressure?

- **Pressure** is defined as

**The force per unit area**

- Pressure is measured in newtons per metre squared (N/m<sup>2</sup>)

  - 1 newton per metre squared is equivalent to 1 pascal (Pa)
  - 1 N/m<sup>2</sup> = 1 Pa
- It can be calculated using the following pressure equation:

$\mathrm{pressure}=\frac{\mathrm{force}}{\mathrm{area}}$

$p=\frac{F}{A}$

- Where:

  - *p* = pressure, measured in newtons per metre squared (N/m<sup>2</sup>) or pascals (Pa)
  - *F* = force, measured in newtons (N)
  - *A* = area, measured in metres squared (m<sup>2</sup>)

- This equation tells us that:

  - If a force is spread over a **large** area it will result in a **small** pressure
  - If it is spread over a **small** area it will result in a **large** pressure
- If an object rests on **more** than one point of contact, add their areas together to get the total area the force is spread over

> **Exam Hint**
> In this course, pressure may also be given in N/cm<sup>2</sup>. If a question provides an area in cm<sup>2</sup>, the pressure can be given in N/cm<sup>2</sup>.

### Examples of applications of pressure

- **Example 1:** Tractors

  - Tractors have **large tyres**
  - This spreads the weight (force) of the tractor over a large area
  - The weight of the tractor is unchanged, so this reduces the pressure and prevents the heavy tractor from sinking into the mud

- **Example 2:** Drawing pins

  - Drawing pins have **sharp pointed ends** with a very small area
  - This concentrates the force, creating a large pressure over a small area
  - This allows the drawing pin to be pushed into a wall

#### Applying a force to a drawing pin

![A thumb pressing a drawing pin into a board, with the large area under the thumb and the tiny area at the board.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/3fdfd42412bf-drawing-pin-v1.png)

*When you push a drawing pin, it goes into the surface (rather than your finger)*

- **Example 3:** High heels

  - High heels have small, sharp points with a small area
  - This concentrates the weight (force), creating a large pressure over a small area
  - Flat shoes have a larger area which the weight (force) is spread over resulting in a lower pressure
  - If the person's weight is the same in both shoes, this explains why high heels sink into soft surfaces more easily than flat shoes

#### The effect of surface area on pressure

![A high-heeled shoe and a flat shoe on soft ground, with the heel producing a much greater pressure because of its small area and the flat shoe producing a much lower pressure because of its large area.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/0b58f1b01a86-4-2-2-pressure-on-different-areas.png)

*High heels produce a higher pressure on the ground because of their smaller area, compared to flat shoes*

> **Exam Hint**
> Note that answers about friction, balance or stability score nothing on a pressure question. Make sure to name the area, the equation and the resulting pressure.

> **Worked Example**
> The diagram below shows the parts of the lifting machine used to move the platform up and down.
> 
> ![A hydraulic lifting machine, with a pump forcing liquid against a piston of cross-sectional area 2.73 × 10⁻² m².](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-igcse-physics-23/assets/24b0a4fa0b97-5-5-1-pressure-worked-example-gcse.png)
> 
> The pump creates pressure in the liquid of 5.28 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa to move the platform upwards. The cross-sectional area of the piston is 2.73 × 10<sup>-2</sup> m<sup>2</sup>.
> 
> Calculate the force that the liquid applies to the piston.
> 
> [2]
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> **Step 1: List the known quantities**
> 
> - Cross-sectional area = 2.73 × 10<sup>-2</sup> m<sup>2</sup>
> - Pressure = 5.28 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
> 
> **Step 2: Write down the relevant equation**
> 
> $p=\frac{F}{A}$
> 
> **Step 3: Rearrange for the force, *****F***
> 
> $F=p\timesA$
> 
> **Step 4: Substitute the values into the equation**
> 
> $F=(5.28\times10^{5})\times(2.73\times10^{-2})=14414.4$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Step 5: Round to the appropriate number of significant figures and quote the correct unit**
> 
> $F=14400N=14.4\mathrm{kN}(3s.f.)$ **[1 mark]**

> **Worked Example**
> A table stands on four legs, and each leg has an area of 100 cm<sup>2</sup>. The table has a weight of 120 N.
> 
> Calculate the pressure on the ground.
> 
> [4]
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> **Step 1: List the known quantities**
> 
> - Area of one table leg = 100 cm<sup>2</sup>
> - Weight = 120 N
> 
> **Step 2: Write down the relevant equation**
> 
> $p=\frac{F}{A}$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Step 3: Calculate the total area of all four table legs**
> 
> $A=4\times100=400\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Step 4: Substitute the values into the equation**
> 
> $p=\frac{120}{400}$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> $p=0.3N/\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
